what_its_for: Filgrastim helps your body make more white blood cells called neutrophils. These cells fight infections. Doctors prescribe this medicine if you have a low white blood cell count, often caused by chemotherapy, bone marrow problems, or certain diseases. It lowers your risk of getting serious infections.
how_to_take: Filgrastim comes as a liquid that is injected under the skin (subcutaneous injection) or into a vein (intravenous infusion) by a nurse or doctor. Your healthcare team will teach you how to give the shot at home if needed. Always inject into a different spot each time, such as the belly, thigh, or upper arm. Never shake the syringe or vial. Use a new needle and syringe every time. Throw away used needles safely in a sharps container — never in the regular trash.
dosing: Your dose is based on your weight and why you are taking this medicine. A common starting dose is 5 micrograms per kilogram of body weight, given once a day. Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to use and for how long. Do not change your dose on your own. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to check your white blood cell count and adjust your dose if needed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, call your doctor or care team right away for guidance. Do not double up on doses. Your blood cell counts need to be monitored closely, so it is important to follow your schedule as closely as possible.
storage: Keep filgrastim in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it — throw it away if it accidentally freezes. Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. You may keep it at room temperature (up to 86°F or 30°C) for up to 24 hours, but then you must use it or throw it away. Do not use it if it looks cloudy, has particles floating in it, or if the expiration date has passed. Keep it out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid touching your injection site with unclean hands. Do not reuse needles or syringes. Avoid crowds and people who are sick, since your immune system may still be weakened while on treatment. Tell your doctor before taking any new medicines, vitamins, or supplements. Avoid getting vaccinations without talking to your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: sudden or severe pain in your upper left belly or left shoulder (could be a spleen problem), chest pain or trouble breathing (could be a lung problem), signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing, fever or chills (signs of infection), unusual bone pain that is very severe, pain or redness at the injection site that gets worse, signs of a blood vessel problem such as sudden leg pain or swelling, headache, vision changes, or confusion.
when_it_works: Filgrastim usually starts working within 1 to 3 days. Your white blood cell count will begin to rise, which helps protect you from infections. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to see how well it is working. You may not feel any different, but the medicine is doing its job in your bone marrow.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The risks and benefits need to be carefully weighed. Children: This medicine can be used in children, and doses are also based on weight. Elderly patients: Older adults can generally use this medicine safely but should be monitored closely. Kidney or liver problems: No special dose changes are usually needed, but your doctor will monitor you carefully. Sickle cell disease: Use with caution, as this medicine may trigger a sickle cell crisis. Always tell all your doctors that you are taking filgrastim.
